The correct choice is Suspend the AZRebalance process in the Auto Scaling Group to prevent rebalancing when the number of instances in each availability zone becomes uneven after terminations. Here’s why:

  • When instances are terminated in a multi-AZ Auto Scaling Group, the AZRebalance process may trigger new instance launches prior to terminating old instances. This is intended to preserve even distribution of instances across availability zones (AZs) and overall high availability. However, this action can result in the ASG temporarily exceeding the desired capacity, as it launches new instances before completing the termination of old ones. By suspending AZRebalance, the group will not try to immediately redistribute capacity, thus preventing this problematic behavior.
  • Change the desired capacity of the Auto Scaling Group according to the number of jobs currently in progress is incorrect, as the application already updates the desired capacity based on job load; the issue isn’t with desired capacity management, but rather with instance distribution logic.
  • Configure all your EC2 instances to launch within a single availability zone is not advisable because it undermines high availability requirements for Paid jobs. Using a single AZ exposes the system to potential outages if that AZ experiences issues.
  • Modify the minimum and maximum capacity of the Auto Scaling Group following the completion of jobs is unnecessary and does not resolve the core problem. Adjusting these limits won’t prevent the ASG from temporarily exceeding desired capacity when attempting to rebalance across AZs.

Tip: Use process suspension (like AZRebalance) for more granular control of how your Auto Scaling Group manages capacity, especially when your workload’s logic already manages scaling based on demand but you need to prevent unexpected launches. Always ensure you understand the impact on availability and resilience.

The best approach is to Deploy an AWS WAF Access Control List (ACL) with a dedicated rule to block incoming SQL injection attempts, then connect this ACL to your Application Load Balancer. AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) allows you to define rules that inspect web requests for SQL injection patterns and block such attacks before they reach your backend servers. Associating the WAF ACL directly to the Application Load Balancer ensures centralized protection for all your EC2 hosts behind it.

Here's why the other options are not suitable:
Set up a WAF Web ACL that allows all web traffic except requests matching SQL injection attack patterns, then link this ACL to every EC2 instance. — AWS WAF can only be associated with CloudFront distributions, API Gateway, ALB, and AppSync, not directly with individual EC2 instances.
Set a policy in AWS Firewall Manager to explicitly block all traffic associated with SQL injection attacks for your EC2 environment. — AWS Firewall Manager is an administrator tool to help manage WAF or Shield policies across accounts, but it does not natively detect or block attacks itself unless used together with WAF rules. You still need WAF rules on the load balancer.
Activate AWS Shield Advanced to stop SQL injection traffic reaching the Application Load Balancer. — AWS Shield (and Shield Advanced) defends primarily against DDoS attacks but does NOT inspect for or block application-layer exploits like SQL injection. Using WAF is the industry standard and AWS-recommended solution for such threats.

Tip: Always associate WAF rules with your application entry point (such as an ALB) to efficiently filter all incoming web traffic before it hits your web servers.

Create two SQS queues: one for high-priority and another for regular messages, processing high-priority queue messages first before handling the normal queue is the best solution. This approach separates image processing requests by priority, ensuring high-priority users or collaborators get their images processed ahead of others as needed. You can configure separate Lambda or EC2-based consumers for each queue, ensuring that the high-priority queue is exhausted before moving on to the normal queue. This strategy efficiently manages workloads and meets stringent SLAs for premium partners.

Here's why the other options are not the most suitable:

  • Distributing both web and application tiers evenly across three availability zones ensures that if an AZ fails, the remaining two AZs retain 4 out of the 6 required instances (or 66%), which satisfies the application’s requirement to function with at least 65% of full server capacity.
  • An ELB (Elastic Load Balancer) and Auto Scaling Groups help automatically redirect and manage traffic and scaling in case of failures.

Let’s clarify why the other options are less suitable:

  • Deploy the web tier across two Availability Zones (AZs) with 3 EC2 instances each, managed by an Auto Scaling Group behind an ELB; deploy the application tier across the same 2 AZs, again with 3 EC2 instances each and an ELB and Auto Scaling Group; use a single RDS instance with read replicas in the second AZ only leverages two AZs, which means a single AZ failure causes a loss of 50% capacity, dropping below the required 65% for the web and app layers. Read replicas also do not provide true high availability as they are not automatic failover targets for RDS in the event of an outage.
  • Distribute the web tier over three AZs, launching 2 EC2 instances per AZ with an Auto Scaling Group and ELB; do the same for the application tier (2 instances per AZ); for the database, create a single RDS instance and deploy read replicas into the other two AZs again fails because RDS read replicas are not used for automated failover. Losing one AZ would mean a 50% drop in capacity, still under the 65% minimum threshold.

Tips: For high availability in AWS, always seek to use as many AZs as are available to increase fault tolerance, combine with Multi-AZ for managed databases, and confirm your instance distribution keeps you above your required operational threshold in the event of an outage.

When you use encrypted Amazon EBS volumes with a supported instance type, encryption is applied to three primary data types:

  • Stored data within the EBS volume itself (data at rest): All data that resides on the encrypted volume is secured via AWS-managed keys or your own KMS keys. This ensures confidentiality even if someone accesses the raw volume.
  • Data transferred between the attached instance and the EBS volume: Data in transit—that is, information moving between your EC2 instance and the EBS volume over the network interface—is protected using encryption, preventing interception or snooping.
  • All snapshots generated from this EBS volume: Snapshots derived from encrypted volumes are also encrypted, maintaining security when stored in Amazon S3.

Here is why the other options are not correct:

  • Information sent from the EBS volume to S3 for storage: While EBS snapshots are stored in Amazon S3, the underlying snapshot handling is automatic and always encrypted when originating from an encrypted volume. Direct copy processes from the volume to S3 do not occur in the way this option suggests, making it inaccurate.

Tip: Remember that AWS EBS encryption is comprehensive for both data at rest, data in transit between the instance and volume, and snapshot storage. Always verify if the instance type supports EBS encryption to ensure full protection.

This configuration automatically reroutes your network traffic through a secure internet VPN if Direct Connect experiences issues, keeping your traffic secure and connected.

Here's why the other options are not as effective:

  • Launch EC2 instances to serve as connection bridges: Simply running EC2 instances does not create network connectivity between AWS and on-premises infrastructure. You need a network link, not just compute resources.
  • Provision an S3 endpoint connection: S3 endpoints allow access to S3 from within the VPC, but they do not enable redundant connectivity between on-premises and AWS core networking services.
  • Add a second Direct Connect link for fault tolerance: While this does provide redundancy, AWS specifically recommends combining Direct Connect with a VPN for true resilience, since both Direct Connect links could still be impacted by provider outages or local failures.

Tips: For best practice, use both a backup VPN and a second Direct Connect if absolute maximum uptime is required.

The Implement a RAID 1 configuration to mirror data across EBS volumes, enhancing EBS fault tolerance. option is correct because RAID 1 provides full data mirroring. This means that data is written identically to two (or more) volumes, so if one EBS volume fails, your EC2 instance can still continue uninterrupted using the mirror. Fault tolerance is key when data is critical, such as in financial systems, and RAID 1 enhances the available protection at the volume level.

Here's why the other choices are not suitable:

  • No action is needed since EBS volumes already guarantee durability by automatically replicating data within one Availability Zone.: While EBS does store data redundantly within an AZ, failures can still occur which impact data availability (e.g., an entire disk failure or AZ issue), so this is not sufficient for high levels of fault tolerance required for mission-critical workloads.
  • Set up multiple EBS volumes in a RAID 0 stripe to ensure greater fault tolerance for your volumes.: RAID 0 only splits data across drives for speed, with no redundancy. If any one EBS volume fails in RAID 0, all data in the array is lost; thus, no fault tolerance is provided at all.
  • Use a RAID 5 configuration across several EBS volumes to boost I/O performance and maintain data redundancy.: While RAID 5 offers redundancy, AWS does not recommend using it with EBS due to high rebuild times and potential performance degradation during a disk failure. RAID 1 is preferred for EBS in critical use cases due to its simplicity and fast rebuilds.

Tip: For the highest data protection on EBS volumes, use RAID 1 or take regular backups via Amazon EBS snapshots. Remember that all RAID is limited to within a single Availability Zone unless otherwise architected, so for even greater durability, also consider cross-AZ replication or backup strategies.

The correct solution is to add an interface VPC endpoint into your VPC for the SaaS application. This will deploy an elastic network interface with a private IP address in one or more of your VPC's subnets, allowing your resources to communicate securely and privately with the SaaS provider over AWS's internal network using AWS PrivateLink. This method keeps the communication out of the public Internet, thus increasing both security and performance.

Let's analyze the incorrect options:

  • In the VPC, create a Direct Connect link for the SaaS in order to connect privately via AWS PrivateLink. – Direct Connect is a dedicated on-premises network link to AWS, but does not replace or enable PrivateLink within a VPC. PrivateLink is used for VPC-to-VPC private connectivity; Direct Connect is for hybrid cloud scenarios, so this won’t solve the requirement in the question.
  • Set up a site-to-site VPN connection in the customer VPC so that the SaaS can use AWS PrivateLink privately. – Site-to-site VPN is for connecting your on-premises infrastructure to AWS, not for connecting to other AWS services or PrivateLink endpoints within the AWS cloud.
  • Configure a gateway VPC endpoint for the SaaS, which attaches an elastic network interface to your subnet using an elastic IP address. – Gateway VPC endpoints are only available for specific AWS services such as S3 and DynamoDB, and do not support elastic or public IPs. For PrivateLink (mostly SaaS, non-gateway AWS services), interface VPC endpoints are required.

Tip: When using AWS PrivateLink to access services from AWS Marketplace or partner SaaS vendors, always create an interface VPC endpoint. Gateway endpoints are not applicable to third-party SaaS offerings or PrivateLink-enabled services, and Direct Connect or VPN are not related to PrivateLink at all for intra-cloud connectivity.

The correct approach is to set the TTL (Time to Live) for the CloudFront cache to 0 seconds. This configuration forces CloudFront to fetch content from the origin for every request, ensuring users always get the latest data whenever the source changes. This setup is the most effective way to ensure dynamic content stays up to date for every client.

The option 'Enable CloudFront's fast invalidation feature' is incorrect because invalidation is mainly intended for purging specific objects from cache when changes are made. However, regular invalidation has some delay and may not guarantee instant updates for every new change.

Choosing 'Configure CloudFront to use a TTL of 10 seconds' will reduce latency for updates compared to higher TTLs, but clients could still receive outdated data for up to 10 seconds after a change, which does not meet the requirement for immediate delivery.

The statement 'Dynamic content cannot be distributed via CloudFront.' is incorrect. CloudFront is capable of handling and delivering dynamic content, especially when properly configured with appropriate cache settings and headers.

Finally, 'Request AWS Support to turn this feature on for your account.' is unnecessary, as managing TTL and cache configuration is entirely user-configurable via the CloudFront console or API—there is no need for AWS support intervention.

Tip: Setting a TTL of 0 seconds can lead to every request hitting the origin server, potentially increasing backend load and affecting performance or costs. Make sure this tradeoff is understood when configuring for dynamic content.

The right way to manage access at the subnet level in AWS is to associate the Network ACL (Access Control List) with the subnet containing the resource—most commonly, this will impact resources like an application load balancer (ALB) in front of the EC2 instances. NACLs operate at the subnet level, not at the resource level, and since an ALB typically fronts the instances in the Auto Scaling group, applying rules to the subnet (and thus affecting traffic to the ALB) is the standard AWS approach.

Assign the Network ACL to the collection of EC2 instances by specifying each instance's ID: This is incorrect, as NACLs are not assigned to individual instances but are subnet-level controls.

Connect the Network ACL to the global CloudFront distribution that delivers content for the product: CloudFront is a global service and does not interact with VPC NACLs directly.

Attach the Network ACL to the Auto Scaling group used by the product: Auto Scaling groups organize and manage instances, but NACLs can't be directly attached to these groups.

Associate the Network ACL with the Network Load Balancer, but only if deployed in US East (N. Virginia): This is misleading; the region does not affect the ability to associate NACLs with resources, and NLBs still inherit NACL rules via their subnet.

Apply the Network ACL to the application's load balancer for the product: This is the best answer, as the ALB typically fronts all traffic going to your application infrastructure, and the NACL on the ALB's subnet will effectively filter incoming and outgoing traffic.

Tip: When you need to control traffic at a network level for scalable web architectures in AWS, always look to secure the subnet containing the public entry point resources (often an ALB or NLB) using NACLs. Security groups, meanwhile, provide instance-level protection.

The observed bottleneck here is due to the instance's EBS-Optimized throughput. Although the total possible IOPS from the EBS volumes increased (6 volumes × 4,000 IOPS = 24,000 IOPS), the instance cannot utilize more because it is capped by its EBS-Optimized throughput bandwidth (500 Mbps). The correct solution is to upgrade the EC2 instance to one with greater EBS-Optimized bandwidth. This allows for more I/O operations to flow between the instance and its EBS volumes.

  • Expanding each EBS volume to 1TB would result in higher Provisioned IOPS supported for each of the six EBS volumes.: While making individual volumes larger allows for higher per-volume IOPS limits, the bottleneck here is not the per-volume IOPS but the total instance throughput.

Set up RAID 0 using just four of the Provisioned IOPS EBS volumes, but increase each to deliver 6,000 IOPS.: RAID 0 can be used with more than four devices. This does not solve the existing throughput bottleneck between instance and storage.
  • Certain block sizes can cause suboptimal I/O throughput. Configure a 64KB block size for the device driver and file system to improve instance throughput.: Block size does impact performance but does not address the main limitation, which is the bandwidth cap between EC2 and EBS.

The best options for reducing backend costs are:

Implement automatic data expiration in DynamoDB using Time to Live (TTL) on records, so obsolete data is cleaned up without manual intervention. — TTL ensures data that is no longer needed is automatically deleted from the table. Since old data isn't required after aggregation, this greatly reduces ongoing storage costs and management overhead. There's no need for manual deletion or complex cleanup scripts.

Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache reads from DynamoDB and lower provisioned read throughputs. — By caching scan results or frequently accessed aggregated summaries, ElastiCache minimizes the number of read requests hitting DynamoDB directly. This can lead to substantial savings in read capacity costs if the same data is accessed often by users.

Why the other options are not ideal:

  • Buffer incoming data in Amazon SQS before writing to DynamoDB to minimize provisioned writes. — SQS doesn’t lower the write throughput to DynamoDB; it only decouples the write process. The total amount written remains, so costs don’t decrease.
  • Allow the app to write directly to DynamoDB instead of uploading JSON files to an S3 bucket. — This may streamline data flow, but it doesn’t address cost optimization. Also, your current design doesn’t indicate the app uses S3 for raw inputs.
  • Switch to storing raw and summarized data solely in Amazon Redshift, eliminating DynamoDB and S3. — Amazon Redshift is best for analytical workloads with complex queries, not for high-velocity transactional use cases like this. Moving everything to Redshift likely increases costs and operational complexity.

Tips: Always look for ways to automatically expire or archive irrelevant data and leverage caching strategies to reduce hot-path database operations. Understand which storage and database types best fit your workload profile to avoid unnecessary expenses.

The Enable the Proxy Protocol through the AWS CLI for the Network Load Balancer to forward the client IP address to the backend service. option is correct.

Here’s why: When a Network Load Balancer (NLB) targets EC2 instances by instance ID and performs TLS termination, the original source IP address is not retained by default for TCP connections. To ensure the backend receives the client's true IP, AWS provides the Proxy Protocol. By enabling Proxy Protocol v2 on the NLB using the AWS CLI, the load balancer appends a header with the client’s IP to the TCP packets, which your backend can then extract and use.

The user must verify that they have been directly permitted to assume the role. This is the essential requirement for a user to switch (assume) roles across AWS accounts. The target role's trust policy must explicitly grant the user or group permission to assume it, typically through the sts:AssumeRole action.

Here's why the other options are incorrect:

  • The account the user intends to access needs to have a custom account alias set up. – Account aliases are optional and make the sign-in URL more friendly, but are not required for role switching.
  • Accessing the role from the source account requires multi-factor authentication (MFA) for the requesting user. – Usage of MFA can be enforced as a policy, but it's not a blanket requirement for switching roles unless specifically set.
  • The user is logged in as a standard IAM user, not as the root user, in their AWS account. – While it's strongly recommended not to use the root account, AWS does not restrict role assumption to only IAM users; root can assume roles technically but it's advised against for best security practice.

Tip: Always set up least privilege permissions, and use trust policies in a cross-account setup to securely enable role assumptions.

answer:
Correct Answer: Establish a single VPC routing table with a default route pointing to the Virtual Private Gateway, and advertise a default route from the on-premises router to AWS using BGP on Direct Connect. Attach this routing table to every subnet.

This is optimal when you want to minimize the number of routes in your AWS routing tables and keep things simple, while maintaining connectivity from both on-premises users and the Internet to your VPC. By propagating a default route via BGP from your customer gateway on Direct Connect, all on-premises branch traffic destined for the AWS VPC will be routed by default, avoiding the need to configure multiple specific routes. Associating this routing table with all subnets ensures a single, unified approach for both Internet and on-premises access.

"Set up two distinct routing tables: one sending default traffic via the Virtual Private Gateway, and the other routing default traffic through the VPN gateway. Assign both routing tables to all VPC subnets." is incorrect because AWS does not support associating multiple routing tables with a single subnet—each subnet can have only one routing table.

"Implement a single routing table including two default routes—one targeting the Internet through a Virtual Private Gateway, and another sending default traffic to the corporate network via the VPN gateway. Use this routing table for all subnets in your VPC." is not valid since routing tables do not allow two default routes (0.0.0.0/0) to co-exist; only one default route is permitted per routing table.

"Create a single routing table containing a default route through the Virtual Private Gateway, and advertise specific on-premises network routes over BGP from the Direct Connect customer router. Link this routing table to all VPC subnets." is suboptimal because advertising specific routes results in a larger, more complex routes table, contradicting the goal of simplifying and minimizing the route entries. Using a default route is more efficient and meets the stated requirements.

Tip: When no additional routing needs are anticipated, leveraging default routes over Direct Connect via BGP significantly reduces the routing configuration overhead and paves the way for easier network management.

The best method to guarantee consistently low latency for Lambda invocations, regardless of the periods of inactivity, is to configure Provisioned Concurrency. With Provisioned Concurrency, you can specify a set number of instances that are kept initialized and ready, ensuring your Lambda function responds immediately even after lengthy periods of no activity. This eliminates cold start delays entirely.

Why other choices are not suitable:

Implement a CloudWatch alarm that monitors function invocations. If there are zero invocations for 60 minutes, trigger the alarm to invoke the function and keep it warm.— While this is a workaround used in the past, it does not guarantee that the function will always be warm when needed, especially if invocations are highly sporadic.

Set up a CloudWatch Event rule to automatically invoke the Lambda function every minute as a way to keep it from becoming idle.— This approach generates unnecessary invocations and could incur additional costs or cause throttling; again, it does not offer fine-grained control, nor does it scale efficiently as demand changes.

Select a language runtime like Node.js or Python for your Lambda due to their shorter cold start times, rather than using Java, which has longer initialization.— While the choice of runtime does impact cold start time, it does not eliminate the problem, and there are applications where Java might be required. It is not a definitive solution and doesn't offer control over concurrent readiness.

Tip: Provisioned Concurrency is purpose-built for controlling and removing Lambda cold start issues and allows you to easily adjust the number of ready instances in response to demand.

Tip: For performance optimization and better user-perceived latency, always focus on caching (where possible), database offloading (via read replicas or caching layers), and edge delivery (CDNs like CloudFront) before aggressive compute scaling for web/application servers alone. The correct answer is "The operation will be denied because the S3 Deny policy in DEV1_OU takes precedence."

Here's why:

  • Service Control Policies (SCPs) act as guardrails at the AWS Organization or Organizational Unit (OU) level. They specify the maximum allowable permissions for all accounts within the OU.
  • If multiple SCPs apply (for example, inherited from parent OUs or explicitly attached), the most restrictive combination is enforced. If any SCP denies an action, it is denied, regardless of what other SCPs allow.
  • Even though Bob's IAM permissions grant him full S3 access and the root SCP is unrestricted, the SCP attached to DEV1_OU explicitly denies S3 actions. This deny cannot be overridden by allows higher or lower in the OU hierarchy or by IAM policies.
  • Therefore, Bob's attempt to access S3 is denied.

Why the other answers are incorrect:

  • "As DEV2_OU allows S3 actions, the request will be permitted due to that SCP's priority." — This is incorrect because Bob is part of DEV1_OU, not DEV2_OU. Only the SCPs for the path to Bob's account apply.
  • "The request will be allowed since Bob's IAM policy has full S3 access and the root SCP is unrestricted." — IAM policies cannot grant permissions that are denied by SCPs. Denies in SCPs always take precedence.
  • "The request will be blocked due to the Admin_OU's SCP denying the operation." — While Admin_OU has a deny, the explicit SCP in DEV1_OU is the effective deny here for S3.

Tip: When tackling SCP questions, remember: explicit deny always wins, even if there are allows elsewhere.

The best ways to reduce ProvisionedThroughputExceededException in DynamoDB are by increasing the provisioned throughput after a CloudWatch alarm detects the exception and adding retry logic in the Lambda function when such exceptions occur. Here’s why these options are correct and others are not:

  • Increase the provisioned throughput when CloudWatch alarms detect failures: This allows your system to automatically raise the read/write capacities when actual demand exceeds current limits, directly addressing periods of high traffic and preventing future exceptions.
  • Incorporate retry logic in the Lambda function: Adding retry functionality helps absorb brief spikes in traffic—most throughput exceptions are temporary, so retrying can often succeed after a short delay.
  • Set up DynamoDB to automatically adjust its read and write capacities via auto-scaling: While DynamoDB auto-scaling can reactively adjust capacity, it may not always respond quickly enough to sudden spikes, making it less effective for immediate resolution.
  • Deploy AWS CloudFront as a cache layer in front of DynamoDB to lessen requests: CloudFront is a CDN designed for static content caching; it isn’t intended to cache or reduce database traffic for DynamoDB, so this won’t help with throughput exceptions.
  • Use an SQS queue to throttle and buffer write operations before sending them to DynamoDB: While SQS can help smooth request spikes, it does not actually increase DynamoDB’s underlying provisioned capacity, meaning queued requests may still cause exceptions once they’re processed unless capacity is also upgraded.

Tips: Use CloudWatch metrics to actively monitor throughput. Combine temporary retries with capacity scaling or on-demand modes to improve resilience against unpredictable spikes.

The correct approach is to Select your API in the API Gateway console, choose Gateway Responses, and update the 403 error response to add custom headers and update the status code to 404. This is because requests to unsupported methods never reach a specific API method integration, so you must customize the Gateway Response sent automatically by API Gateway when encountering such scenarios.

Let's review each option:

  • Configure the API method's integration response to include your custom headers and change the status code to 404. - This would only work for valid methods; unsupported methods never invoke a specific integration response, making this ineffective for the described case.
  • Select your API in the API Gateway console, choose Gateway Responses, and update the 403 error response to add custom headers and update the status code to 404 - This option directly addresses the Missing Authentication Token (403) error by allowing you to modify the default Gateway Response to return 404 and attach the required headers.
  • Locate the Missing Authentication Token response under Gateway Responses in the AWS API Gateway console, and change it to forward an HTTP 404 status with your additional headers. - While this statement is on the right track, API Gateway 'forwards' errors internally through the Gateway Responses customization, not by 'forwarding' as suggested; the process is simply to edit the response mapping, not to forward errors between types.
  • Open the integration response for your API method, and set up a mapping to return a 404 Not Found error and insert your headers there. - Unsupported HTTP methods never reach the integration response, so this option would not affect the error in question.

Tip: For errors handled by API Gateway itself (not your integration), always use the 'Gateway Responses' feature to customize status codes and headers. Integration and method responses only help for successful method matches.

Leverage Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service), which natively offers scalable pub/sub message distribution without fixed limits. is the best answer. SNS is AWS's managed publish/subscribe messaging service. It's designed to scale seamlessly and can broadcast messages to multiple subscribers or endpoints (HTTP, Lambda, SQS, etc.), just like the Redis pub/sub pattern your application currently uses. It is ideal for delivering real-time bidding and price notifications to multiple interested services or clients.

Here's why the other options are less suitable:

  • Select Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) standard queue...: SQS standard queues are optimized for message processing with high throughput, but are point-to-point (producers send, consumers receive) instead of publish/subscribe (broadcast to multiple consumers).
  • Set up an SNS FIFO queue...: As of now, SNS only supports standard (non-FIFO) topics. There is no such thing as an SNS FIFO queue, so this isn't a viable choice.
  • Implement SQS FIFO queues and change the bidding event handler to Lambda...: While SQS FIFO queues are helpful for strict ordering and deduplication, they don't provide a publish/subscribe pattern required for auction event broadcasting. Also, involving Lambda solely for event routing adds unnecessary complexity.
  • Use SQS FIFO queue's message group identifier feature...: Message group IDs are useful to preserve order for related messages within a queue, but this still doesn't allow broadcasting the same message to multiple subscribers/channels simultaneously.

Tip: When replacing Redis pub/sub, always look for AWS services that support true publish/subscribe messaging patterns. SNS is purpose-built for this, whereas SQS is primarily for decoupling applications through queuing and message processing. Always check latest AWS documentation as features may evolve.

The scenario states both departments are tagging, so DLM applies both policies to the shared volume when both tags exist.

Incorporate the runtime interface client within the container image so that Lambda can recognize and invoke your function. This is mandatory when building custom container images for AWS Lambda. Let's consider why the other choices are incorrect:

Leverage AWS Direct Connect to transmit information, then persist it in Amazon S3. is the most optimal solution for sending large, recurring data sets (measured in gigabytes) from multiple worldwide locations to AWS for storage and analysis. This reduces latency and can eliminate bottlenecks caused by variable internet performance, making it highly suitable for regular, high-volume transfers.

Why the other options are not ideal:

However, it is not practical for daily transfers from multiple global locations because the device needs to be physically shipped and handled.
  • Send the files using S3 Transfer Acceleration, storing them in Amazon S3. – S3 Transfer Acceleration uses AWS edge locations to speed up data uploads over the public internet, but its effectiveness depends on internet quality and can be costlier for sustained, high-volume workflows. It is more suitable for occasional or geographically diverse uploads, not high-frequency, large-scale, cross-site transfers.
  • Transfer and archive the data via S3 Transfer Acceleration into Amazon Glacier. – Glacier is designed for long-term archive storage, not for active, frequent data analysis. Additionally, using S3 Transfer Acceleration for Glacier is not a supported nor an optimized workflow.

Tip: For organizations with ongoing, predictable high-volume data transfer needs, especially with global presence, Direct Connect coupled with Amazon S3 ensures better performance, security, and cost efficiency over the long term compared to internet-based methods or physical devices.

  • API Gateway enforces a non-modifiable 30-second timeout for requests. Gateway-Cached Volumes allow you to keep your most frequently accessed data locally, while storing the full dataset durably in Amazon S3. This approach greatly minimizes the on-premises storage footprint and maximizes cost-efficiency by leveraging AWS's scalable storage while still providing quick access to active data.

Here are breakdowns for the alternatives:

The Gateway-Stored Volumes configuration is usually more suitable than Gateway-Cached Volumes, and thus should be preferred as the backup storage medium. — This is incorrect because Gateway-Stored Volumes keep the entire dataset on-premises and only asynchronously back up to AWS, making it less cost-effective since it requires you to maintain substantial local storage hardware.

For cost-effectiveness, you must utilize the Gateway-Virtual Tape Library (VTL) exclusively. — This is not ideal, as VTL is particularly designed for companies with existing tape backup processes and does not necessarily offer the lowest cost for all scenarios.

Either Gateway-Stored or Gateway-Cached Volumes can be used, but both should be paired with the Gateway-Virtual Tape Library (VTL) for the optimal storage solution. — Combining these solutions increases complexity and cost without adding value over using just Gateway-Cached Volumes for a typical backup scenario.

Tip: In backup scenarios, prioritize solutions that limit local storage requirements and leverage AWS S3 for scalable and inexpensive long-term retention.

When the stack is deleted, setting DeletionPolicy to Retain ensures the S3 bucket remains and is not deleted with the stack. Using Snapshot for the RDS instance means a final backup will be created; this snapshot can be used to restore the database later. This enables future restoration of both data and storage objects, aligning with your manager’s request for recovery.

Examining the options:
"Add Replication to the S3 bucket to copy the objects elsewhere and configure the RDS instance with a DeletionPolicy of Snapshot." – While this ensures a copy of the S3 data, replication is unnecessary here; DeletionPolicy directly on the bucket suffices.
"For both RDS and S3 resources in the CloudFormation template, set the DeletionPolicy to Retain." – This keeps both resources, but for RDS, Snapshot is preferable, since it allows you to later restore using a valid database snapshot instead of leaving a potentially unused RDS instance.
"Specify the Snapshot DeletionPolicy for both S3 and RDS resources in the CloudFormation stack." – S3 buckets do not support the Snapshot DeletionPolicy. Only RDS supports creating snapshots. For S3, use Retain to preserve data.

Tips: The "Retain" DeletionPolicy prevents a resource from being deleted when its stack is removed. RDS supports the "Snapshot" DeletionPolicy, which generates a snapshot upon deletion instead of immediate removal. Always map these policies according to resource type.

The two supported validation options for AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) public certificates are email-based validation — where ACM sends messages to the contact email addresses listed in the WHOIS records of the domain, and DNS-based validation — where you add a specific CNAME record to your domain's DNS configuration. Both of these provide assurance that you control the domain in question.

  • Email-based validation (option: ACM dispatches a confirmation email...) is supported; you need to follow ACM's email instructions to complete validation.
  • DNS-based validation (option: You can use DNS-based verification...) is supported. You publish an ACM-supplied CNAME, and ACM automatically checks DNS to confirm ownership.

Incorrect statements include 'ACM automatically issues SSL certificates for domains on Route 53, requiring no further validation from your side.' and 'If your domain is enrolled with Route 53, merely clicking the Pending Validation icon...', neither of which are valid ACM behaviors: you must still complete either DNS or email validation regardless of where your domain is registered. 'ACM sends an SMS text to the domain owner's registered phone number...' is not a method ACM supports for validation.

Tips: For automation and to streamline renewals, DNS validation is preferred; it doesn't require re-approval when certificates are renewed. Email validation can be delayed if domain contact emails are outdated or inaccessible.

Activate AWS WAF to safeguard the application against DDoS attacks. is the best and most straightforward solution for this scenario. AWS Web Application Firewall (WAF) is specifically designed to protect web applications from malicious common web exploits as well as DDoS attacks. It is easy to integrate with existing AWS services like ELB and CloudFront, and gives you flexible rule-based controls to allow, block, or monitor (count) web requests. It is also cost-effective, managed, and scalable—meaning AWS handles all the operational heavy lifting for you.

Why the other choices are less effective or incorrect:

  • Advise the company to use a Direct Connect partner facility and set up a 1Gbps Direct Connect link to their VPC.: This is mainly intended for improving private connectivity and bandwidth between the data center and AWS, not designed to block DDoS traffic. Setting this up is neither cost-effective nor an actual DDoS mitigation approach.
  • Manually block the previously identified attacker IP addresses by creating explicit DENY entries in a Network ACL on the subnet hosting the web tier.: NACLs are difficult to manage at scale during a DDoS attack—attackers can leverage many IPs, and managing deny rules is cumbersome, quickly exceeding NACL limits. This method isn't scalable and is not sufficient for DDoS mitigation.
  • Remove support for all protocols but TLS 1.0 & 1.2 on the web-tier ELB and turn on Advanced Protocol Filtering, thus allowing ELB to serve as a web application firewall.: Elastic Load Balancers (ELBs) don't natively provide WAF-like functionality via protocol filtering, and disabling other protocols or only allowing TLS doesn't address DDoS attacks.
  • Set up Internet access at a co-located facility, use a hardware-based WAF to filter incoming traffic, and tunnel traffic into the VPC over Direct Connect.: This is complicated and costly to operate, requiring physical hardware, extra networking, and isn’t a quick or cost-effective counter to DDoS events.

Tip: AWS provides automated protections such as AWS Shield Standard by default to all customers, but setting up AWS WAF allows you to tailor application-level rules and get enhanced DDoS defense in a flexible, pay-as-you-go model.

This dynamic adjustment helps maintain application performance and cost-efficiency. However, it is important to understand that Auto Scaling operates by adjusting the quantity of instances, not their type or size.

The option Switch to a larger EC2 instance size if CPU usage rises above a threshold is incorrect because Auto Scaling does not upgrade or resize existing EC2 instances; Instance resizing (vertical scaling) requires manual intervention or separate services such as EC2 Instance Refresh or AWS Elastic Beanstalk.

Similarly, Reduce to a smaller EC2 instance type if the workload lessens is not supported by Auto Scaling groups. Instead, Auto Scaling enables horizontal scaling—adding or removing instances according to demand, based on configured policies and CloudWatch alarms.

Tip: When optimizing for Auto Scaling, focus on scaling out (adding more instances) or scaling in (terminating instances) based on performance metrics to meet demand efficiently.

This policy, called "Match Viewer," permits CloudFront to mirror the protocol used by the viewer when connecting with the origin. If a user visits via HTTP, CloudFront uses HTTP to reach the origin; if HTTPS, CloudFront uses HTTPS as well. This ensures flexibility and can be helpful in scenarios where both protocols must be supported.

The option Restrict CloudFront to only use HTTPS for connections to the origin. forces all communication to happen over HTTPS, preventing HTTP from being used and thus not allowing both protocols. Meanwhile, Configure CloudFront to use exclusively HTTP for origin connections. does not meet the requirement of supporting both HTTP and HTTPS. The statement There is no protocol policy that enables both HTTP and HTTPS communication. is incorrect, as the "Match Viewer" policy is explicitly designed for this use case.

Tip: Remember that the "Match Viewer" policy in CloudFront Origin Settings is the option that lets CloudFront communicate with the origin using the same protocol (HTTP or HTTPS) as the viewer request!

The best solution is Set up AWS Storage Gateway using Gateway-Cached volumes to present local block storage with cloud-backed scalability. Gateway-Cached volumes let you keep frequently accessed data locally, while storing the full dataset in Amazon S3. This approach supports POSIX block access, allows a large (624TB+) dataset to be presented as a single mountable LUN, and enables users to access portions of data during backup since only hot data is cached onsite.

Point your backup application at Amazon S3 as its destination for data backups is incorrect because backup software that requires block-based POSIX storage cannot write directly to an S3 bucket, which is object storage. Similarly, Have your backup application target Amazon Glacier directly for all backup jobs is not possible as Glacier is archival object storage and does not support direct mount or POSIX block semantics. Deploy Storage Gateway using Gateway-Stored volumes to mirror all data locally before uploading to AWS would require all 624TB to be stored on-premises first, defeating the purpose of scalable cloud storage and not offering the same caching efficiency of Gateway-Cached volumes.

Tip: Use Gateway-Cached volumes when you want scalable cloud-backed storage but only require local access to the most frequently used data.

This approach allows you to tailor the load that each ELB directs to the underlying instances according to their capacity. Since c5.2xlarge instances are much more powerful than large instances, you can assign Route 53 weights so the c5.2xlarge ELB handles a greater proportion of incoming traffic, fully utilizing those instances while the large RIs are fully loaded. This strategy makes the best use of available instance capacity and reserved capacity costs.

Why the other options are not optimal:

  • Establish Auto Scaling with ELB to add up to 10 more on-demand large instances whenever CloudWatch detects full utilization or to shut off c5.2xlarge instances. – This could lead to unnecessary costs since purchasing additional on-demand large instances defeats the purpose of maximizing the already-procured c5.2xlarge RIs. Also, turning off c5.2xlarge instances would waste their unused capacity.
  • Configure two c5.2xlarge instances behind the ELB and use Auto Scaling with on-demand c5.2xlarge instances for up to two extra servers. – Managing all servers as only c5.2xlarge reduces the usage of existing large RIs and could increase costs. The question also specifies maximizing the effectiveness of both instance types, not just scaling c5.2xlarge.
  • Direct Route 53 to send traffic straight to large and c5.2xlarge EC2 instances, using latency-based routing and health checks to bypass the ELB. – This undermines the benefits of ELB, which provides health checks, session stickiness, and easier scaling. Routing directly to EC2 also complicates management and reliability.

Tip: When you have a mixed fleet of instances behind a load balancer with significantly different capacities, use weighted routing techniques to ensure more traffic goes to the larger instances so you maximize efficiency and cost-effectiveness.

The Route53 ALIAS record pointing to your ELB's DNS name is the recommended solution. By integrating an ELB, you ensure that all traffic to your Auto Scaling group of web servers is load balanced, fault-tolerant, and able to scale with demand. Using a Route53 ALIAS record allows you to map your custom domain directly to the ELB—this is preferred over CNAME at the apex domain level and removes the need to hardcode ELB DNS names or IPs.

Here's why other answers are incorrect:
"Configure a CloudFront distribution with your web servers' private IPs as origins and point a Route53 CNAME record to the CloudFront distribution."—CloudFront cannot use private IPs residing within a VPC as origins without help from a public-facing load balancer, and this approach doesn't harness the scaling and health checking of ELB.
"Assign Elastic IP addresses to all the web servers and set up a Route53 A-Record with these EIPs and enable DNS failover with health checks."—This increases manual management and defeats the purpose of Auto Scaling, limiting scalability and requiring human intervention.
"Deploy all web servers behind an Elastic Load Balancer."—While this is a step in the right direction, it doesn’t specify how end-users would access the ELB through DNS. Direct access via ELB DNS name isn’t user-friendly. Integrating with Route53 completes the best practice.
"Create a NAT instance within your VPC, set a default route through the NAT instance, and point a DNS A record to its public IP."—A NAT instance is intended for facilitating outbound internet access for private subnets, not for handling inbound web traffic from users. Configuring DNS to point users to a NAT instance provides no web application access.

Tip: Always integrate load balancers with Route53 for highly available and scalable architectures. Use ALIAS records for apex domains. Keep manual intervention to a minimum by leveraging automation and scalable services.

The right answer is Leverage synchronous master-standby database replication between two different Availability Zones. Using synchronous replication ensures that changes are immediately copied to a standby node in a separate Availability Zone. In the event of failure (such as data corruption or hardware/software issues), failover can occur rapidly (within the required RTO of 3 hours, typically much less). Since replication is synchronous, the data on both nodes stays consistent, helping you meet the RPO of 15 minutes—even if the corruption happened 10 minutes ago, the standby node will not have diverged.

The correct process is to produce a copy of the EBS snapshot, encrypt the new copy with CMK-B, then use this to generate an AMI and deploy the EC2 instance in the production account. This is required because EBS snapshot encryption cannot be changed in place: you have to create a copy while specifying a new KMS key (in this case, CMK-B) to re-encrypt the data. This guarantees that the production instance’s volumes are encrypted with the intended key for the production environment.

The other options are incorrect for the following reasons:

  • Share the existing encrypted snapshot from Account A directly with Account B, keeping the encryption key as CMK-A, and utilize it for launching the EC2 instance: This would result in Account B’s volume still being encrypted with CMK-A, not the correct key for production (CMK-B).
  • Create an image (AMI) in Account B from the shared snapshot, but leave the underlying encryption key unchanged: Like the previous option, this doesn't transition encryption to the production CMK, which is a key requirement.
  • Simply launch a new EC2 instance in Account B using the AMI created from the original snapshot without re-encrypting the volume: Volumes will still be encrypted with the development key, defeating the security isolation between accounts.
  • Launch the instance directly using the existing image, and then change the encryption key for the EBS volume after deployment: AWS does not permit changing an EBS volume's encryption key in place; you must perform a snapshot copy and re-encrypt instead.
  • Copy the EBS snapshot to another snapshot without encryption and share it with Account B before launching the EC2 instance: Encrypted EBS snapshots cannot be converted into unencrypted snapshots; encryption must remain, and the key can only be changed through snapshot copying with the new KMS key.

Tip: When migrating encrypted AMIs or EBS snapshots across AWS accounts, always remember to create a snapshot copy using the destination account’s required KMS key for proper encryption and resource isolation.

The right approach in this scenario is to Export your MySQL database data to a newly provisioned EBS volume attached to the EC2 instance, utilizing migration or disk management tools. Instance store volumes are ephemeral, meaning their data is lost when the instance stops, terminates, or fails. To ensure persistent and reliable backups, you must copy your critical data off the instance store and on to a durable storage service. EBS volumes, unlike instance store, survive instance restarts and can be snapshotted for disaster recovery.

Why are the other options not recommended?

  • Initiate a backup of the database's file storage directly to an Amazon S3 bucket: While backing up to S3 is valuable, directly backing up the raw database filestore (rather than using a logical data export, such as mysqldump) can risk inconsistent or corrupt backups, especially while the database is running. Best practice is to use proper MySQL export or backup tools to guarantee data consistency before storing in S3.
  • Use the EC2 console's instance 'Create Image' feature to generate an AMI, thus capturing MySQL data present on the instance store: AMIs capture EBS volumes attached to an EC2 instance, but do not persist data residing on instance store volumes. Thus, using this method does NOT back up your MySQL data if it resides only on the instance store.
  • Take a direct snapshot of the instance store volume hosting the MySQL database and replicate the snapshot to different AWS regions for redundancy: AWS does not allow snapshots of instance store volumes. Snapshots are only supported for EBS volumes, so this approach is technically infeasible.

Tip: Any application storing persistent data on instance store volumes should regularly export important data to persistent storage, such as EBS or S3. Consider running databases on EBS for data durability whenever possible.

  • BGP ASN for dynamic routing: This value is only necessary when the routing option for the VPN is Dynamic (using Border Gateway Protocol), as BGP uses ASNs to facilitate interaction between the AWS side and your customer gateway.
  • Static, routable public IP address: AWS must be able to always reach the customer gateway device over the Internet. Hence, the IP must be static and globally routable—not a private or dynamic IP—so AWS knows where to establish the VPN tunnel each time.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A BGP ASN if you are using static routing: Static routing does not require BGP ASN input because BGP will not be configured for this type of connection.
  • A dynamic public IP address is needed for your customer gateway or the NAT device, if one is present: Dynamic IP addresses are not supported for the customer gateway device. The IP address must be static so that AWS can maintain a consistent VPN endpoint.

Tip: Double-check whether your customer gateway device is directly Internet-facing or if it requires NAT. Either way, the configured IP must still be static and publicly routable. If you are unsure about routing choice, remember that BGP ASN is only relevant for dynamic VPNs—static VPNs don't need it.

The Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1) EBS volume is designed for workloads that demand very low latency, consistent and high IOPS performance, and high throughput. Such volumes justify the higher cost where storage operations are critical to application success.

Among the options, the Cassandra database system with strict requirements for extremely low latency and consistent, high-performance storage is the scenario where io1 is most appropriate. This is because database workloads like Cassandra's often require stable, reliable, and fast disk performance—something that general-purpose SSD or magnetic volumes cannot reliably deliver under heavy workloads.

The other options are not ideal for io1:

  • Some large, infrequently accessed legacy data used only for occasional audits, with minimal daily read activity. - This workload can be hosted on Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) or even Cold HDD (sc1) volumes, which are far more cost-effective for rarely accessed data.
  • The main disk of a testing server that is regularly utilized by the QA department. - For boot volumes or environments where workload is moderate and performance needs aren't critical, General Purpose SSD (gp2 or gp3) are suitable options.
  • A data warehouse for customer analytics where big datasets are frequently scanned and processed by monitoring scripts. - Data warehouses primarily need high throughput, not high IOPS. Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) is typically the best fit for such requirements, allowing large-scale, sequential access efficiently and cost-effectively.

Tip: Reserve io1 volumes for databases or applications with high transaction rates and strict performance SLAs. Leveraging other volume types for less demanding storage needs can generate substantial cost savings.

The best practice for file-level restore when you have frequent EBS snapshots is to create a new EBS volume from the snapshot, attach it to your EC2 instance as a secondary volume, browse to find the deleted or lost file, and simply copy that file from the secondary volume back to the original one. This allows you to recover individual files quickly—usually well within the 15-minute window—since volume creation and attachment from a snapshot generally completes in just a few minutes.

Here's why the other options are not ideal:

  • "Initiate a cron process to regularly run 'aws s3 cp' and upload your EBS volume files to S3 for backup." — This method suggests copying EBS volume files to S3, which is not a viable backup or restore strategy for block storage devices, as it might lead to inconsistencies. Moreover, it is not suitable for swift, file-level recovery from snapshots.
  • "Stop the current frequent EBS snapshotting. Then, create a volume from an existing snapshot, attach it to the EC2 instance at a different mount point, update your application to use the new backup volume, and detach or delete the original volume." — This option involves cutting over to a backup volume entirely, which is unnecessary and can cause more disruption. It also halts ongoing snapshots, which can compromise your backup strategy and reduce resilience.
  • "Provision a new EC2 instance from the latest EBS snapshot and transfer the necessary system files from this fresh instance over to the original EC2 instance." — Spinning up a whole new instance just to recover a file is time-consuming, costly, and introduces unnecessary complexity, especially since you can simply mount the snapshot as a volume directly to the existing EC2 instance.

Tips for similar scenarios: Always leverage EBS snapshot restore workflows for granular recovery. Mounting a volume from snapshot at a secondary mount point ensures minimal disruption, quick restore, and precise retrieval of needed files.

  • With Multi-AZ configurations, Amazon RDS maintains a synchronous standby replica. If an AZ becomes unavailable, RDS quickly fails over to the standby in another AZ with minimal downtime. This ensures the database is immediately restored to its latest consistent state without manual intervention, which is crucial for high-availability and disaster recovery tests.

Why the other options are less suitable:

  • Promote a read replica to a standalone instance, and update the application...: Read replicas are typically asynchronous and may lag behind the primary instance. Promoting a read replica doesn't guarantee zero data loss and may not have the absolute latest data, so this does not ensure the most recent state.
  • Recover the database by restoring from the most recent automated snapshot...: Automated snapshots only capture the database up to the backup interval and do not include data changes that happened after the last snapshot. This could lead to significant data loss if recent transactions are not included.
  • Leverage the RDS Copy Database feature to clone...: There is currently no native feature named 'Copy Database' in RDS. The cloning process is also similar to restoring from a snapshot, so recent transactions may not be reflected. This process doesn't guarantee up-to-the-minute restoration.

Tip: For critical workloads, always use Multi-AZ RDS deployments to benefit from automatic failover and the best possible recovery point in case of AZ-level failures.

The correct answer is ELB passes requests through without altering the HTTP headers.

When a Classic Load Balancer is set up to use an SSL listener for backend communication, it forwards the request as-is and does not modify the request headers. This means all custom headers and original information sent by the client are preserved. Understanding this preserves application transparency and avoids troubleshooting confusion when apps expect unaltered headers.

Let's review the incorrect choices:
- ELB can inject requester information by changing headers for the backend. - This is incorrect because Classic Load Balancer does not inject or alter client headers at the HTTP layer when using an SSL listener.
- ELB will intercept incoming requests if sticky sessions are in use, adding its own cookie information. - While sticky sessions (session persistence) can involve cookies for HTTP/HTTPS listeners, for pure SSL listeners, the ELB does not insert cookies or modify packet contents.
- You cannot set up both the ELB and backend servers to listen for SSL traffic at the same time. - This is false; both can be configured for SSL, and the connection is secured end-to-end.

Tip: When working with Classic Load Balancers and SSL, remember that header modification only occurs for certain types of listeners (e.g., HTTP/HTTPS), not pure SSL (TCP) listeners.

To introduce IPv6 into the existing VPC, you first need to attach an Amazon-assigned IPv6 CIDR block to both the VPC and its subnets. This can be easily accomplished in the AWS VPC console by selecting "Add IPv6 CIDR." After this, each subnet within the VPC can be assigned its own IPv6 block. Secondly, you'll need to configure proper routing for IPv6 traffic. For public subnets, routes should direct all IPv6 traffic (::/0) to the VPC's internet gateway. For private subnets, security dictates that you direct outbound IPv6 traffic to an egress-only internet gateway, which allows NAT-like one-way internet access for IPv6 traffic (since NAT gateways are not compatible with IPv6). Thirdly, it's essential to assign IPv6 addresses to each EC2 instance from the subnet's allocated IPv6 range in order for those instances to communicate over IPv6.

The following options are incorrect:
Delete the current VPC and set up a new VPC with both IPv4 and IPv6 CIDR blocks, then create new subnets supporting both address types: This is unnecessary, as AWS allows you to add IPv6 addresses to an existing VPC and subnets without needing to recreate them.
Edit route tables so public subnets send IPv6 traffic to the internet gateway, and private subnets send IPv6 traffic to a NAT gateway: NAT gateways work only for IPv4 traffic and are not supported for IPv6. For IPv6, you must use an egress-only internet gateway for private subnet outbound traffic.
Assign IPv6 addresses to NAT gateways so that EC2 instances in private subnets can use them for outbound IPv6 connectivity: Assigning IPv6 addresses to NAT gateways is not possible nor supported. NAT gateways function only for IPv4, not for IPv6. Always use an egress-only internet gateway for IPv6 in private subnets.

Tips: Remember that enabling IPv6 in AWS VPC environments does not require deleting or recreating the VPC or subnets—just associate an IPv6 CIDR and adjust routing. NAT gateway does not support IPv6; always choose an egress-only internet gateway for IPv6 in private subnets. Ensure EC2 instances have IPv6 addresses assigned to communicate using IPv6.

The most effective approach is to use Configure an ElastiCache cluster and implement logic to cache the relevant dynamic content before querying the MySQL database to accelerate access times. ElastiCache provides an in-memory cache that sits in front of the database, allowing frequently accessed dynamic data to be served rapidly without hitting the database each time. This reduces load on the MySQL instance and significantly improves application responsiveness for end users. When dealing with substantial dynamic content, database-level caching is the ideal strategy because web caches (such as CloudFront) are generally optimized for static content or easily cacheable dynamic responses.

The option Leverage Route 53 as your DNS; its global DNS infrastructure will reduce DNS lookup latency by routing users to the nearest DNS endpoint. is not an effective solution for caching dynamic web application content, as DNS-based optimization only impacts domain lookups and has negligible effect on actual application data delivery or RDS query performance.

With Set up a CloudFront distribution, enable query string forwarding, and configure the cache TTL to zero... and Provision a CloudFront distribution, turn off query string forwarding, and adjust the TTL to zero..., both options would result in essentially no caching of content (TTL set to 0) and only potentially offer connection reuse to the origin. However, for high-volume dynamic content, CloudFront does not natively provide appropriate caching for personalized or frequently changing data, so it will still forward almost all requests to the origin database. These methods will not achieve the intended caching benefits and do not address the primary caching use case described in the scenario.

Tip: For dynamic applications with intensive database workloads, use ElastiCache or similar technologies specifically designed for data caching—especially where database query results can be reused—even for short durations. Edge caching and DNS optimizations don’t adequately tackle the latency or scalability challenges for high-frequency, dynamic, database-driven content.

The correct choice is Enhanced networking. This feature provides significantly higher bandwidth, lower latency, and lower jitter for your EC2 instances compared to traditional network interfaces. By utilizing enhanced networking, especially with the Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) or Intel 82599 Virtual Function (VF) interfaces, you remove many performance bottlenecks typically associated with network communication between EC2 clusters within the same region.

Why other options are incorrect:
Cluster placement group: While placement groups can help optimize network performance by grouping EC2 instances within a single Availability Zone, they do not remove bandwidth limitations between clusters. The question specifically asks about communication between clusters.
Amazon PV AMI: Paravirtual (PV) AMIs are generally less performant than HVM and do not benefit from enhanced networking capabilities.
Amazon HVM AMI: Hardware Virtual Machine (HVM) AMIs are required for enabling enhanced networking, but just selecting an HVM AMI alone doesn’t guarantee maximum performance—it is the activation of enhanced networking that makes the key difference.
Amazon Linux: This is an operating system, not a networking or placement feature, so it does not address network performance improvements alone.
Amazon VPC Endpoints: VPC endpoints allow private connectivity to AWS services without using public IPs, but they are not designed for improving EC2-to-EC2 network performance.

Tips: To fully leverage enhanced networking, ensure both your instance type and AMI supports the appropriate network driver. Also, remember that combining enhanced networking with placement groups can further boost performance for tightly-coupled applications.

The correct answers are "Sign in as the root user of your Organization and send invitations to external AWS accounts, which must then accept to be added." and "In the AWS Organization's management console, directly create new AWS accounts within your Organization's structure."

  • With AWS Organizations, you can centrally manage and create new accounts under your Organization directly from the console, which is helpful for greenfield scenarios ("In the AWS Organization's management console, directly create new AWS accounts within your Organization's structure.").
  • Alternatively, you can invite existing AWS accounts to join your Organization. This is done by the Organization's management (root) account, which sends an invitation. The owner of the target account must log in and accept the invitation ("Sign in as the root user of your Organization and send invitations to external AWS accounts, which must then accept to be added.").
  • The option "Have users from external accounts sign in to the AWS Organization console with their root credentials and submit a join request to your Organization's administrator." is incorrect, as AWS does not provide a 'join request' feature directly from external accounts using the console. The invitation must come from the Organization, not the joining account.
  • "Configure a cross-account IAM role that allows access to the Organization and have users assume this role to call the add-account-to-organization API operation." is not a supported method; accounts cannot join by assuming a cross-account role and calling an Organization API without first being invited.
  • Finally, "Run the AWS CLI command request-join-to-organization from the member accounts. Once the owner approves, the accounts will join the organization." is not accurate. There is no such CLI command or flow for joining from the member side; the process always starts with an invitation from the Organization's root account.

Tip: Always initiate adding accounts to an AWS Organization from the management account, either by creation or invitation. Externally-owned existing accounts must explicitly accept the invitation before joining. Also, avoid attempting to script joining operations from the prospective member account.

The best and fastest way to temporarily block traffic from a specific IP address range for all incoming connections in a VPC is to update the Network ACLs on all public subnets in the VPC to explicitly block the suspicious IP address range. Network ACLs are stateless and evaluated before traffic hits any EC2 instances or security groups, providing a centralized, subnet-level method to block traffic based on IP, protocol, or port. This makes them ideal for quickly mitigating threats, such as port scans, from a specific block of IPs.

The option Deploy a policy in Active Directory to push Windows Firewall changes to all hosts within the VPC to reject incoming traffic from that IP block is incorrect because not all hosts may be joined to Active Directory, and using AD policies is a complex and time-consuming approach—definitely not suitable for quick, temporary mitigation.

The choice Manually update the Windows Firewall rules on every AMI used in the VPC to block the malicious IP addresses is also inefficient. Updating the firewall on every running instance or future instances based on an AMI is slow, error-prone, and difficult to revert after 24 hours.

The option Attempt to add a deny rule for the suspicious IP block to all VPC Security Groups is not valid, as Security Groups are 'allow-only'—they do not support explicit deny rules. This makes them unsuitable for rapidly denying access to malicious IPs.

Tips: For network-level protection, Network ACLs offer both allow and deny rules and operate at the subnet level—perfect for temporary or emergency blocks. Security Groups, on the other hand, are stateful and can only be used to allow traffic. Choose Network ACLs for subnet-wide, quick blocks when you need to act fast!

  • Deploy an endpoint service using AWS PrivateLink inside the provider’s VPC: AWS PrivateLink allows services in the provider VPC to be privately shared with many client VPCs, minimizing exposure and simplifying the architecture, especially for large numbers of customers.
  • Other AWS client accounts can connect from their VPCs to the endpoint service by setting up an interface VPC endpoint: Customers can securely establish connections from their own VPCs directly to the endpoint service using PrivateLink, ensuring traffic stays within the AWS private network.

Why the other options are less suitable or incorrect:

  • Establish a VPC peering connection between the provider’s VPC and each client’s VPC for secure and private communication: While VPC peering does enable private connectivity, it becomes unmanageable at scale (over 300 VPCs); route table limitations and transitive peering restrictions are significant drawbacks.
  • Install a virtual private gateway within the provider’s VPC: A virtual private gateway facilitates VPN or AWS Direct Connect connections—not the best fit for direct AWS-to-AWS VPC connectivity at scale.

Tips & Tricks: For situations with a large number of VPCs requiring private access to a central service, always evaluate PrivateLink for its scalability, security, and simple management compared to alternatives like VPC peering or VPNs.

Amazon S3 assigns each object a distinct encryption key and secures this key using a main master key that S3 maintains and regularly rotates. This is the most accurate description of Server-Side Encryption with Amazon S3-Managed Keys (SSE-S3), also known as SSE-S3. In this approach, S3 automatically handles both the creation and management of the encryption keys for each object, and provides robust encryption using unique keys per object. The keys themselves are protected by a master key, which is periodically rotated to uphold strong security standards.

Looking at the incorrect options:

  • S3 enables you to control and administer your own encryption keys, while managing the encryption and decryption process onsite. — This actually describes SSE-C (Server-Side Encryption with Customer-Provided Keys), not SSE-S3, as SSE-S3 does not allow you to manage your own keys.
  • Distinct permissions and auditing functionality exist for the envelope key, enhancing security and tracking of key usage. — This aligns more with SSE-KMS (Server-Side Encryption with AWS KMS Keys), where envelope encryption integrates with KMS for granular permissions and audit trails.
  • You are provided with a randomly created data encryption key by Amazon S3 to encrypt your data before uploading. — In SSE-S3, S3 handles all key management and encryption transparently; customers are not supplied with or responsible for any encryption keys directly for encrypting/uploading data.

Tip: Remember, the main feature of SSE-S3 is that Amazon S3 fully manages the keys and rotation, giving you straightforward encryption at rest without having to design or administer a key management workflow yourself.

Deploying a t2.medium instance as a 3-year Reserved Instance (RI) provides significant cost savings, especially for long-running workloads that show infrequent performance spikes. The t2.medium uses the burstable CPU model, letting it handle occasional higher loads while remaining resource- and cost-effective during idle times. By selecting a 3-year RI, you maximize discounted rates for your steady-state legacy app.

"Run two t2.nano instances, each equipped with Single Root I/O Virtualization" sounds cost-effective but is operationally complex, and splitting workloads across multiple nanos offers limited benefit for a single legacy application that can't be distributed or scaled.
"Use a t2.nano instance and extend capacity with spot instances only during peak demand" is unreliable for legacy applications that may not gracefully handle interruptions or scaling, especially since spot instances can be reclaimed by AWS at any time. To ensure even distribution of traffic across multiple availability zones, you should take the following steps:

  • Enable cross-zone load balancing: With this feature, the load balancer will distribute traffic evenly to instances in all registered AZs, regardless of the originating AZ. Without cross-zone load balancing, the load balancer may direct traffic only to instances within a single zone, resulting in uneven distribution.
  • Use two or more availability zones behind the load balancer as recommended by AWS: AWS best practices recommend registering healthy instances from at least two (preferably more) different AZs behind the load balancer. This increases the application's fault tolerance and ensures requests are routed broadly.

Why are the other options incorrect?

  • Lower the frequency at which health checks are performed: The frequency of health checks does not impact traffic distribution. This setting only affects how quickly unhealthy instances are detected and replaced.
  • Turn off sticky sessions on the load balancer: Since your application doesn't require client requests to be sent to the same EC2 instance, sticky sessions are not necessary. However, enabling or disabling sticky sessions won't resolve uneven AZ load distribution; it affects how traffic is routed to instances rather than to AZs.

Tip: For proper load balancing across availability zones, always enable cross-zone load balancing and ensure you have healthy instances in all desired zones registered with the load balancer.

The best solution is to define groups in Amazon Cognito User Pool, associate each group with an IAM role, and assign users to groups according to their required access. This approach leverages Cognito's built-in group and role mapping features to manage permissions efficiently and at scale. Each group (e.g., reader, contributor, editor) gets an associated IAM role with the minimum necessary permissions, and users inherit those permissions by joining groups.

Option 'Set individual IAM policies directly on users in Amazon Cognito User Pool to ensure each user has permissions matching their role.' is not recommended, because Cognito does not support attaching IAM policies directly to individual users inside User Pools—permissions are managed at the group level with IAM roles. Option 'Create corresponding groups and permissions structures in IAM, and then assign each Amazon Cognito user to these IAM groups to control access.' is incorrect since IAM groups are intended for use with AWS IAM users, not Cognito User Pool users, and IAM groups cannot be linked to Cognito users or their authentication process. Option 'Establish multiple IAM roles for each type of user, then assign users their respective IAM role directly from Amazon Cognito User Pool.' is also not the ideal method, as Cognito assigns permissions by associating IAM roles to groups, not directly to individual users.

Tip: When using Cognito with AWS resources, always manage user authorization through group-to-role mappings for efficiency, scalability, and maintainability.

The correct approach utilizes Amazon Kinesis to collect streaming sensor data—a service purpose-built for handling high-throughput, low-latency real-time workloads like ingesting data from thousands (and scaling to millions) of devices. Kinesis provides the ingest layer necessary to later enable real-time dashboards, a future requirement.

Here's why this solution works best: Kinesis efficiently buffers incoming data, and it can directly deliver batches to Amazon S3 for archival and batch processing. S3 lifecycle policies can then transparently transition older data to Glacier, meeting archival requirements without extra management overhead. In parallel, EMR can be triggered to perform ETL on the Kinesis input or its output in S3, transforming and cleaning the data before loading it into Redshift for reporting and analytics.

Why the other choices are less suitable:

"Store sensor data in Amazon S3 with lifecycle policies..."—Using S3 as the direct landing zone is scalable for batch storage but not ideal for ingesting rapid, continuous, streaming data from millions of devices. There is also limited real-time ingestion capability compared to Kinesis.

"Use Amazon Cognito to receive incoming data..."—Cognito is designed for identity management and authentication, not for mass data ingestion or streaming. While it can help with device pairing, it’s not practical or scalable as a data input mechanism, nor is it a fit for high-frequency sensor uploads.

"Persist data directly to a scalable DynamoDB table..."—DynamoDB can handle high write throughput, but storing all raw, high-frequency time-series data from millions of sensors could quickly become costly and unnecessarily complex. It's typically better for structured, indexed access patterns rather than raw event streaming and archiving. There’s also no direct native support for streaming into S3/Glacier.

Tips: Always match AWS services to the data’s velocity and volume. Choose Kinesis for real-time and streaming ingestion at massive scale, S3 for cost-effective storage and archiving, Glacier for long-term retention, EMR for scalable processing (ETL), and Redshift for high-performance analytics/reporting.
