The 20.0.0.255 IP address is not assignable to any EC2 instance in this VPC, because it serves as the broadcast address for the 20.0.0.128/25 subnet.

For your subnets:
- Public (20.0.0.0/25): IPs range from 20.0.0.0 (network address, not assignable) to 20.0.0.127. The usable host addresses are 20.0.0.1 - 20.0.0.126, since .0 (network), .127 (broadcast), and AWS reserves the first 4 and last 1 addresses of the subnet.
- Private (20.0.0.128/25): IPs range from 20.0.0.128 (network address, not assignable) to 20.0.0.255 (broadcast address, not assignable). Usable host addresses are 20.0.0.129 - 20.0.0.254 (again, AWS reserves the first 4 and last address).

20.0.0.255 is, thus, unassignable.

The other choices:

- 20.0.0.132: Falls within the private subnet's range.
- 20.0.0.122: Falls within the public subnet's range.
- 20.0.0.55: Falls within the public subnet's usable range.

Tip: Remember that every subnet reserves its network and broadcast address (plus some AWS-reserved addresses), so not all IPs in a range are valid for EC2 instances. Always check subnetting boundaries to ensure you don't select a reserved or out-of-range address.

Tip: When restoring workloads with specific storage requirements (such as file-level, block-level, or tape-based storage) on AWS, carefully map storage gateway configurations to your application access requirements—VTL for backup/restore archives, file/iSCSI for live application access.

To successfully migrate a MySQL database from on-premises to AWS RDS and keep the databases in sync using AWS Database Migration Service (DMS), the following three steps are essential:

Set up a replication instance using AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) and allocate enough CPU and memory resources to ensure migration operations complete efficiently: The DMS replication instance carries out the migration and handles reading from the source and writing to the destination. Proper sizing ensures performance and avoids bottlenecks.

Create one or more migration tasks specifying which tables or schemas to migrate and enable the option to migrate both existing data and synchronize ongoing changes: Selecting 'migrate existing data and replicate ongoing changes' guarantees that not only will the initial data set be migrated, but any subsequent changes will also be captured and applied. This keeps both environments synchronized until cutover.

Define both a source and a target database endpoint in DMS, using the on-premises MySQL database as the source and the Amazon RDS MySQL instance as the target. Select 'MySQL' as the engine for each endpoint: Endpoints are required so DMS knows where to read the data from and where to write it.

The following options are incorrect:
Launch an EC2 instance to act as a processing server for DMS and assign it a role that grants access to the RDS database. In DMS, configure this EC2 instance as the replication host: DMS does not use a traditional EC2 instance as a replication server; instead, DMS manages its own replication instances.
When configuring your migration in DMS, simply select the source as the on-premises database and the engine as 'MySQL'; DMS will automatically create the destination endpoint within your chosen subnet: You must explicitly specify both the source and target endpoints. DMS cannot automatically create the target endpoint without configuration.

Tips:

  • Always ensure your replication instance is adequately sized for your data volume and throughput needs.
  • For ongoing synchronization, choose the migration type that supports both full and ongoing data replication.
  • Accurately configure both source (on-premises) and target (RDS) endpoints, including connectivity details and engine types.

This can be achieved by configuring either Cognito User Pools as an identity provider, or by utilizing Cognito Identity Pools (federated identities) to authorize users via Google.

The "Amazon Cognito Identity Pools (federated identities) support user authorization with federated identity providers, including Google, Facebook, Amazon, and SAML. Set up federated identities for Google to permit sign-in." option is correct because Cognito Identity Pools (federated identities) enable secure user access to AWS services (like DynamoDB) using external identity providers such as Google for both iOS and Android platforms. The "Cognito User Pools enable user authentication with federated identity providers such as Google, Facebook, SAML, and Amazon. To use Google, federated identities must be configured within the User Pool." option is also valid, as Cognito User Pools now support federation with external identity providers, allowing developers to configure Google as an identity provider for web or mobile applications.

The incorrect choices are:

  • "Only iOS (Objective-C and Swift) supports federated identities with Google through Cognito, by configuring identity pools with a Google Client ID." This is not accurate; both Android and iOS platforms can leverage Cognito with Google federation, not just iOS.

To deliver content over HTTPS from a custom domain using CloudFront, you'll need to provide a valid SSL certificate for your domain. The recommended and cost-effective method is to use Server Name Indication (SNI) Custom SSL on your CloudFront distribution. SNI allows CloudFront to serve multiple SSL certificates on the same IP, which supports modern browsers and reduces costs compared to dedicated IP SSL certificates.

The other options are incorrect for these reasons:

  • Set up an ALIAS record in Route 53 and link it to your CloudFront distribution: While an ALIAS record is needed to map your custom domain to CloudFront, this step alone does not provide SSL/TLS security or cover the requirement to support HTTPS with your custom domain.
  • Obtain and configure a custom SSL certificate in Route 53, then associate it with your CloudFront distribution: Route 53 is primarily a DNS service and does not manage SSL certificates for CloudFront. SSL certificates for CloudFront distributions must be obtained through AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and associated directly with the distribution, not Route 53.
  • Build an Origin Access Identity (OAI) for CloudFront and assign appropriate permissions to your S3 bucket: OAIs are used to restrict S3 access to only CloudFront, which enhances security, but does not address serving content with a custom domain over HTTPS.

Tip: Always use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for provisioning SSL certificates in AWS, and associate them with your CloudFront distributions for your custom domain. SNI Custom SSL is free and suitable for most use cases.

This approach enables URL-based filtering—critical in this scenario because access control based solely on IPs, ports, or protocols (as is the case with security groups and network ACLs) cannot restrict outbound requests based on URL or DNS name. By routing all outbound traffic through a web proxy, you can enforce precise policies that allow only requests matching the DNS names or URLs of the permitted software servers.

The other options are insufficient for the following reasons:

  • "Set up security groups with outbound rules that only permit connections to the update servers." — Security groups can filter on IP addresses and ports but lack the capability to filter traffic by URL or DNS name.

  • "Configure network ACLs to grant outbound access solely to required destinations, applying implicit deny for all other routes." — Like security groups, network ACLs filter only on IP and port, not DNS or URL, and thus are unable to restrict traffic based on dynamic DNS-based endpoints.

Tip: For VPCs needing URL or domain-based egress filtering, always consider a proxy solution (e.g., Squid, AWS Network Firewall with FQDN rules, or AWS Cloud-based proxies). This allows fine-grained control well beyond what native VPC constructs like security groups and NACLs can provide.

Tip: Always double-check for protocol support differences when porting legacy network-dependent applications to AWS, and consider overlay networking solutions when native support is unavailable.

AWS VPC strictly enforces non-overlapping subnet CIDRs within each VPC, so the second subnet cannot be created.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • Having a subnet with the same CIDR as the VPC is not permitted.

To hibernate an EC2 instance, several criteria must be satisfied. First, The root volume for the EC2 instance must be backed by Amazon EBS and not by instance store. This is mandatory, since hibernation depends on an EBS volume to persist the contents of RAM and the instance state. The root storage volume needs sufficient capacity to store the data from memory (RAM). If the root EBS volume lacks adequate space, the memory snapshot required for hibernation won't fit and the hibernation process will fail. Instances that are part of an Auto Scaling group or managed by ECS cannot be hibernated. AWS restricts hibernation for instances that are managed dynamically, as hibernation involves persisting a unique memory and instance state which could be problematic in scalable or containerized environments.

Why the other options are incorrect:
- The Mac OS AMI being used on EC2 must offer support for hibernation. – Hibernation is not supported for Mac OS EC2 instances; the feature is available for certain Linux and Windows instance types only.
- Hibernation requires that the root volume is not encrypted since this would disrupt the RAM data restore process. – This is not the case. In fact, instance root EBS volumes are supported whether they're encrypted or not, and RAM data is encrypted with AWS Key Management Service (KMS) during hibernation. There is no need to avoid encrypted volumes.

Tip: Always verify that the instance type, AMI, and EBS volume size are compatible before enabling hibernation. Ensuring that the root volume has enough capacity for memory snapshot is a common mistake that can cause hibernation to fail.

The best answer is Set up an Elastic Load Balancer with TCP listeners on port 443 and route traffic to the web servers behind the ELB. When you need HTTP clients to be authenticated with client certificates, this process must occur at the web server. Using an ELB with a TCP listener (Layer 4) allows SSL/TLS negotiation—including client certificate authentication—to terminate at the web server, not at the ELB. This enables the server itself to validate the client's certificate.

Let's review why the other options do not meet the requirements:
Configure your web servers as the backend targets of a CloudFront distribution and utilize your custom SSL certificates on CloudFront: CloudFront supports custom SSL certificates but does not support client certificate authentication to backend servers.

Deploy an Elastic Load Balancer with HTTPS listeners and place the web servers in the backend pool: An ELB with HTTPS listeners terminates SSL at the ELB, meaning only the ELB sees the client certificate, and the backend servers never get it for validation.

Tip: Always use an ELB with TCP listeners for scenarios requiring full SSL handoff and client-side authentication at the application/web server layer.

The recommended design is to leverage Amazon S3 for storage of input and output files, use SQS queues for passing processing tasks, and set up an Auto Scaling group of servers that dynamically scales based on SQS queue depth. This approach is optimal for several reasons:

  • Amazon S3 offers virtually unlimited, highly durable, and cost-effective storage, making it the right choice for both input and output files without worrying about storage limits or performance bottlenecks during peak hours.
  • Amazon SQS provides a robust, scalable message queue that decouples message producers (file uploads) from message consumers (processing instances). This allows flexible workload distribution and smooth handling of spikes in input volume.
  • Auto Scaling ensures that the number of processing instances matches the workload by tracking the SQS queue depth, providing elasticity during usage peaks and saving on costs otherwise.

Why the other options are not ideal:

  • Store files in EBS volumes with Provisioned IOPS, send image processing tasks using SNS to a group of instances, and use Auto Scaling to match the number of hosts to the number of SNS messages.
    While EBS with PIOPS provides performance, EBS volumes don't scale as automatically or cost-effectively as S3 for large, shared file access, and SNS is not designed for reliable task queuing where processors need to pick up and process jobs independently. SNS is push-based and can lose messages if subscribers aren't available.
  • Deploy S3 buckets for storing files and SNS topics to fan out processing tasks to multiple servers, with Auto Scaling responding to the count of SNS notifications.
    Again, SNS lacks message durability and guaranteed delivery per processor seen with SQS. SNS is appropriate for notification or fan-out, but not for guaranteed, distributed task processing requiring reliable queue semantics.
  • Place files on EBS with PIOPS for performance, distribute task commands through SQS to multiple processing servers, and scale the number of servers up or down in proportion to SQS queue length.
    EBS does offer good IOPS performance, but it's more costly and hard to use at scale for scenarios with large, rapidly changing data sets and requires manual management of volumes across instances. S3 is preferred for the scalable, stateless pattern expected here.

Tips & Insights: Always use S3 for scalable and high-durability file storage, SQS for distributed, reliable task queues, and Auto Scaling with metrics (queue depth) to handle sudden spikes in workload efficiently and at optimal cost.

The correct way to enable hibernation is to launch a new instance with hibernation configured at creation using a supported HVM AMI. You can't enable hibernation on existing EC2 instances that were launched without the hibernation flag and required configurations (such as suitable AMI, enough root volume space, and compatible instance type).

The option "It is not feasible to enable hibernation on an existing instance. You must launch a new EC2 instance using an HVM AMI and specify the hibernation setting on the instance configuration screen." is correct. This is because hibernation requires both an HVM (Hardware Virtual Machine) AMI and that the instance be launched with the hibernate flag enabled at creation.

Reviewing the distractors:

  • "You can use the AWS Management Console to pick the existing instance and choose Actions → Instance State → Stop - Hibernate." – This is incorrect because hibernation has to be enabled at launch. Existing instances without this setting can't suddenly support hibernation via the console.
  • "You can only set the hibernation option on running instances via AWS CLI by executing "aws ec2 hibernate-instances --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0"; the AWS Console does not support hibernation." – This is also incorrect. Both AWS Console and CLI support hibernation if enabled at launch. Plus, simply running a CLI command on an instance that wasn’t prepared for hibernation will not suffice.
  • "To allow hibernation, you must terminate the existing instance and create a new one using an instance store volume." – This is misleading; not only do you need a new instance, but the storage must be EBS-backed (not instance store) for hibernation to work. Instance store volumes cannot be hibernated, as data in memory would be lost at shutdown.

Tips and Insights:
  • Hibernation snapshots memory to the EBS root volume. For this to work, extra space in the root EBS volume is required.
  • Always check for AMI compatibility and set hibernation at the time of creation if you plan to use it.
  • Read AWS documentation to understand EC2 features and limitations before launch.

The main reason for this 502 (Bad Gateway) error is usually related to the configuration of the SSL/TLS certificate at the Origin. If the certificate is expired, invalid, or not signed by a trusted authority, CloudFront will be unable to establish a secure connection to your origin when HTTPS is used. This results in a 502 error.

The correct option clearly mentions that the SSL/TLS certificate at the origin may have expired or not been signed by a third-party Certificate Authority. To resolve this, ensure the certificate is valid and issued by a reputable CA.

The following options are incorrect for these reasons:
There is a permissions issue preventing users from logging in to the web application.—This pertains to authentication within the application and would not cause CloudFront to show a 502 error at the CDN layer.
HTTPS is enabled for the CloudFront origin, but HTTPs is not enabled on the CloudFront distribution.—CloudFront would not attempt HTTPS to the origin unless configured, and this mismatch would result in other errors, not necessarily a 502 specifically.
A Lambda function in the request validation chain failed to execute correctly, resulting in the error.—While a Lambda@Edge failure could influence responses, it does not typically result in a 502 unless specifically coded to return such status, which is less common than certificate misconfigurations.

Tip: Always verify that your origin's SSL certificates are valid, correctly chained, and trusted by Amazon CloudFront.

The best solution is to Set up an instance as a reverse proxy ahead of your web servers, and deploy IDS/IPS agents on each such proxy node. Placing IDS/IPS at the reverse proxy layer allows you to efficiently inspect incoming Internet traffic before it reaches your application servers, minimizing overhead and centralizing detection and prevention capabilities. This architecture streamlines monitoring and response, fitting AWS best practices for scalable security.

The option Enable SSL listeners on Elastic Load Balancers in front of your application servers (Elastic Load Balancing with SSL listeners) is primarily used for encrypting traffic, not for active network traffic inspection or threat detection/prevention. Tip: Always look for centralized, scalable security layers in AWS architectures, and be aware of the limitations of VPC networking, such as the lack of promiscuous mode. By turning on sticky sessions in your Elastic Load Balancer, you instruct AWS ELB to bind a user session to one instance, ensuring all the user's requests are sent to the same target during their session. This approach needs minimal effort—simply enable the feature—and adds no extra infrastructure or significant cost.

Configure Elastic Load Balancing to generate its own session cookie and define a custom stickiness period if your application does not use its own session cookie is not the best first step, as the basic sticky session capability with ELB (using the application's own cookie or the AWS-generated cookie) is already simpler and faster for typical web workloads. Customizing the cookie configuration is an advanced option, but not necessarily the quickest for the majority of cases.

Turn off the sticky session setting and use ElastiCache for session storage, which allows centralized, scalable, and managed in-memory session state is more complex and potentially costlier, as it involves deploying extra infrastructure and modifying your applications to store session information in ElastiCache, which is not the most cost-effective for simple session stickiness.

Implement a custom tracking cookie for each request to each ELB listener to identify the target instance, relying on the load balancer to look for this tracking information adds unnecessary complexity, as AWS ELB already provides built-in sticky session features. Custom coding cookies and managing them for each request is not as efficient or scalable.

Tip: For most basic session persistence needs on ELB, enable stickiness using the existing features and resort to centralized session management (such as ElastiCache) only if you need cross-instance/session fault tolerance or your application is highly stateless.

Establishing IPsec tunnels between on-premises infrastructure and an Amazon VPC with Virtual Private Gateways and customer gateways delivers several key security features:

  • Ensures both endpoints confirm each other's identity before the VPN connection is established. — IPsec VPN setup mandates mutual authentication using pre-shared keys or certificates, enabling each side to verify who they are communicating with. This is essential for trusted connectivity.
  • All data transferred over the VPN is encrypted as it travels across the public Internet. — The primary benefit of IPsec is that it encrypts payloads, ensuring confidentiality of information even as it passes through untrusted networks.
  • Automatically verifies that the data sent is not altered during transit across the Internet. — Through cryptographic integrity checks and hashing mechanisms (such as HMAC), IPsec assures the integrity of data packets, protecting against unauthorized modification in transit.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Achieves end-to-end data security from your on-premises application to the application running in AWS. — This is misleading. IPsec protects data 'in transit' over the Internet, but does not secure it within the client or server environments on either end. True end-to-end encryption would require application-layer controls.
  • Guarantees that only authorized users at either end of the VPN tunnel can access specific AWS resources. — While IPsec authenticates networking endpoints (gateways), it does not provide granular user-based access controls for AWS resources. Identity and authorization for AWS resources are managed separately (such as via IAM).

Tip: Remember, IPsec VPNs focus on protecting the data in transit—offering encryption, endpoint authentication, and integrity—between your networks, but not at the application or user level.

When you place a Lambda function into a private subnet, it loses internet access by default because private subnets do not have a direct route to the internet. To restore internet connectivity for resources in a private subnet, you should use a NAT gateway in a public subnet, and update the private subnet's route table to send outgoing traffic through it.

The correct answer is: Configure the private subnet's route table to send outbound traffic through a NAT gateway that resides in a public subnet. This setup allows the Lambda to reach the internet for necessary outbound communication (such as API calls to external services) while still being able to access resources inside the VPC, like the RDS database.

Why the other options are incorrect:

Set up VPC endpoints for all required AWS services the Lambda function needs — This could help for AWS services that support PrivateLink, but it will not restore general internet connectivity (for example, if Lambda needs to reach public APIs, this will not help).

Leave the Lambda function outside the VPC to retain default internet access — While this would give Lambda internet access, it prevents direct connectivity to your RDS instance within the VPC, which is required by the scenario.

Assign an Internet Gateway directly to the public subnet connected to your VPC — An internet gateway is required for internet access from a public subnet, but attaching it alone doesn't provide internet access to private subnets. The NAT gateway setup is what bridges this.

Update the route table to direct all inbound and outbound traffic through the Internet Gateway — This would make a subnet public. For security reasons, databases and their associated Lambda functions are kept in private subnets. Routing all traffic via an internet gateway would defeat the purpose of the private subnet and is not recommended.

Tip: Remember, for internet-bound traffic from resources in a private subnet, always use a NAT gateway (or NAT instance) in a public subnet.

This approach fully meets the security requirement that documentation must not be available directly via S3.

Here's why the other approaches are incorrect:

  • Establish a dedicated IAM user for CloudFront, giving the user access rights to your S3 bucket contents: CloudFront doesn't authenticate as an IAM user. IAM users are for individuals/applications, not AWS-managed services like CloudFront.
  • Configure an S3 bucket policy that specifies the CloudFront distribution ID as the Principal, and the bucket's ARN as the resource: S3 bucket policies do not permit distribution IDs as valid principals – they require AWS service principals (like OAIs) or IAM ARNs.
  • Assign specific access policies to each S3 bucket containing the documents, limiting permissions so that only CloudFront can reach them: While this might seem possible, S3 doesn't natively recognize CloudFront as a direct principal for access; OAIs are the mechanism by which CloudFront is authorized.

Tip: Always use Origin Access Identities (or Origin Access Control for new distributions) to protect S3 content behind CloudFront, ensuring S3 serves objects only to CloudFront and not directly to the public.

answer:
The best approach is to use a standard SQS queue as the dead letter queue (DLQ), thereby allowing problematic messages to be isolated for further investigation and troubleshooting. In this scenario, since the main queue is a standard queue, you should create another standard queue as the DLQ. Standard queues support high throughput and at-least-once delivery, and this setup enables you to divert unsuccessfully processed messages after a certain number of failed attempts, simplifying troubleshooting and preventing the main queue from getting cluttered with problematic messages.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Increase the visibility timeout slightly and monitor logs to see if problems with message processing persist. – While adjusting the visibility timeout can sometimes help if your processing jobs take longer than expected, it does not isolate failed messages, and will not help with repeated processing failures.
  • Set up a new FIFO queue as a dead letter queue to store messages that fail to be processed. – FIFO queues require all sources and target DLQs to also be FIFO. Since the main queue in this scenario is a standard queue, only another standard queue can be used as its DLQ.
  • Adjust the visibility timeout to 0 to reduce the effects when message deletion does not succeed. – Setting visibility timeout to 0 would make messages immediately available for other consumers, which could result in multiple reprocessing attempts and increase the risk of duplicate processing. This does not help in isolating the failed messages.

Tip: Always pair the dead letter queue type with the source queue type (Standard with Standard, FIFO with FIFO) in SQS. Leveraging DLQs is a best practice for isolating and diagnosing troublesome messages without impacting the main processing workflow.
